messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus had spent twenty-three years building a career around the safety of children. As principal of a mid-sized elementary school in suburban Ohio, he prided himself on knowing every face in his hallways, every squeaky hinge on every door. He was the kind of man other people described as unflappable. That changed on a Tuesday afternoon in late October when he was walking to his car in the school parking lot after a late budget meeting. A man he did not recognise approached him from behind a row of vehicles, demanded his keys and wallet, and when Marcus hesitated — not out of defiance but out of sheer disbelief — struck him twice across the face and throat with what turned out to be a heavy metal flashlight. Marcus fell between two cars, unable to call out, staring up at the gap of darkening sky above the roofline while footsteps retreated across the asphalt.

He did not lose consciousness, but he lost something else. In the weeks that followed, Marcus found that the memory of the assault refused to behave the way memories were supposed to. When he tried deliberately to reconstruct what had happened — sitting with a detective, later with his wife — the details slipped away from him, assembling themselves only in fragments and out of order. He could not reliably describe the man's face or the sequence of blows. Yet without any conscious effort, the memory would return on its own terms: a film that simply began playing, the crunch of gravel underfoot, the cold metal against his jaw, his body curling instinctively onto its side — and in those moments he could feel his shoulders drawing up and his neck contracting, his torso folding exactly as it had between those two cars. The body remembered what the mind could not retrieve on demand.

It was through these unbidden replays that the world began to feel dangerous in a new and specific way. Each time the memory surged back — triggered by the scrape of a chair leg, the particular quality of light on a parking lot surface, the sound of footsteps behind him — Marcus emerged from it with his nervous system already primed for attack. The replays did not feel like recollection; they felt like evidence that the threat was still present and ongoing. His startle response became severe enough that a student dropping a tray in the cafeteria could send him lurching sideways against a wall. He began scanning every room he entered for its exits — the gymnasium, the staff meeting room, the church he and his wife attended on Sundays — cataloguing doors within the first seconds of arrival. His eyes moved constantly to objects that could be used as weapons: a letter opener on a secretary's desk, a fire extinguisher mounted in the corridor, a stapler left on a conference table. He was not choosing to do this. He was certain, at some level beneath argument, that the assault was not over.

His occupation placed him in direct and daily contact with the very environment where it had happened. Every afternoon, when the last bell rang and staff began filtering to the parking lot, Marcus found reasons to stay inside. He rescheduled walkthroughs, lingered over paperwork, waited until the lot was empty before crossing it — and even then he walked close to the building wall, his back never fully turned to open space. His assistant principal had begun quietly covering duties that required him to be outside. His wife, Elena, had noticed that he no longer sat with his back to the restaurant door, that he had stopped attending the evening neighbourhood association meetings he once chaired, that he flinched when she touched his shoulder unexpectedly. She had asked him, carefully, whether he was sleeping. He had told her he was fine.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a morning when a seventh-grader — a boy who had done nothing wrong — ran up behind him in the hallway and Marcus spun around and grabbed the child by the collar before he understood what he was doing. He stood there, the boy's eyes wide, and felt something clarify. He was most afraid, he said at intake, that he had become someone dangerous inside the building he was supposed to make safe. What he hoped for, more quietly, was to be able to walk to his own car again without rehearsing his own death.
